title: Google graded the grades
whisper: Their verdict, in their own words.
source: Laszlo Bock to The New York Times, June 2013
_note: Rendered in raea (raea/ungraded-006-gpa): a paper diorama on a desk, pop-up standees, one continuous camera; cues live in the composition.

beats.say: That's Laszlo Bock, Google's head of people, in The New York Times, {2013|twenty thirteen}.
Grades and test scores? "No correlation at all." Only a slight one for brand-new grads.
And after two or three years, how you do at Google is "completely unrelated" to how you did in school.
Brainteasers? "A complete waste of time." They mostly made the interviewer feel smart.
So Google stopped asking most people for transcripts.
Some Google teams were {14%|fourteen percent} people with no college background.
Here's what "no correlation" looks like. Line people up by GPA, then by how well they do the job.
If grades predicted the job, you'd get a line. Instead, you get a cloud.
School grades your answers to someone else's questions. A job asks you to find the questions.
Careful: that's one company, one interview, in {2013|twenty thirteen}. Plenty of employers still check grades.
But the lesson travels. Out here, people stop asking what you scored. They ask what you can show.
Picture two applicants. One sends a {4.0|four point oh}. One sends a link to something they built, broke, and fixed.
The grade says you passed. The thing you built says you can.
So keep your grades. Build something too. Because one day, someone runs the numbers. Like when…
